      <content name="title">Body Weight</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">BMI</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Overweight</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Underweight</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is body weight?<p>Body weight is the total mass of your body. Keeping track of your weight is one way to check for changes in your health, but it can't tell you the whole story. That's because your weight includes muscle, bone, <span class="qt0">fat</span>, and water. Also, everyday factors can play a role in your weight, such as your:</p><ul><li>Diet</li><li>Activity level</li><li>Stress level</li><li>Sleep habits</li><li>Family history and genetics</li><li>Age</li></ul>What factors help determine a healthy body weight?<p>A healthy weight is more than just a number on the scale. It's about feeling good, having energy, and lowering your risk of disease. Your health care provider can help you determine a healthy body weight based on several factors. These include your:</p><ul><li>Body Mass Index (BMI). BMI is a measure of how much you weigh compared to how tall you are. The higher your BMI, the higher your risk for certain diseases. BMI does not distinguish between <span class="qt0">fat</span>, muscle, and bone mass. It also may overestimate body <span class="qt0">fat</span> in athletes or those with a muscular build, or underestimate body <span class="qt0">fat</span> in older persons or others who have lost muscle.</li><li>Waist circumference. If most of your body <span class="qt0">fat</span> is around your abdomen (belly) rather than your hips, you may be at a higher risk for heart disease and type 2 diabetes.</li><li>Health history. Your health care provider will likely consider your risk factors for diseases and health conditions, such as having high cholesterol, in determining your healthy body weight.</li></ul>What are body weight ranges?<p>Having a healthy body weight may lower your chance of developing certain health problems. Carrying too much or too little weight can affect your health. Ranges of body weight include:</p><ul><li>Underweight. Your weight is lower than it should be for your health.</li><li>Normal. Your weight is within a healthy range.</li><li><span class="qt0">Overweight</span>. Your weight is greater than it should be for your health.</li><li>Obese. Your body <span class="qt0">fat</span> is greater than it should be for your health.</li></ul><p>Body weight needs can be different at different ages. For children, weight and growth are tracked over time based on their age.  For older adults, keeping muscle and strength is key, and sudden weight loss should always be checked by your provider.</p>What if I have a sudden gain or loss of weight?<p>Talk to your provider if you're losing or gaining weight without trying. A sudden, unexpected change in weight can be a sign of a medical problem.</p><p>Causes for sudden weight loss can include:</p><ul><li>Thyroid problems</li><li>Cancer</li><li>Infectious diseases</li><li>Digestive diseases</li><li>Certain medicines</li></ul><p>Causes for sudden weight gain can include:</p><ul><li>Certain medicines</li><li>Thyroid problems</li><li>Heart failure</li><li>Kidney disease</li><li>Liver disease</li></ul>How can I maintain a healthy body weight?<p>Maintaining a healthy body weight can improve energy, sleep, and overall wellbeing. Talk to your provider about what a healthy weight would be for you. If they recommend that you gain or lose weight, they might refer you to a dietician for support. A dietician is a professional who has special training to help you learn the best way to eat.</p><ul><li>Good nutrition and exercise can help in losing weight. Even a small change in weight can lower your risk of developing certain diseases.</li><li>Eating extra calories within a well-balanced diet and treating any underlying medical problems can help you gain weight.</li></ul><p>Focus on your health, not just the number on the scale. With daily healthy habits and self-compassion, you can support lasting improvements in your overall wellbeing.</p><p>NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/obesity.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Obesity</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Overweight</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0">obesity</span>?<p><span class="qt0">Obesity</span> is a disease that means having too much body <span class="qt0">fat</span>. It is different from being <span class="qt0">overweight</span>, which means weighing too much. Both terms mean that your weight is greater than what's considered healthy for your height.</p><p>Body Mass Index (BMI) measures how much you weigh compared to how tall you are. An adult who has a BMI of 30 or more is considered to have <span class="qt0">obesity</span>. Severe <span class="qt0">obesity</span> is having a BMI of 40 or higher. <span class="qt0">Obesity</span> increases your risk for many other diseases and health problems, especially if the extra body <span class="qt0">fat</span> is carried around the waist.</p>What raises your risk of <span class="qt0">obesity</span>?<p><span class="qt0">Obesity</span> happens over time from taking in more calories (through food and drinks) than used up from physical activity and daily living. Your body stores the extra calories as <span class="qt0">fat</span>. The right balance between calories and activity is different for everyone.</p><p>There are many different factors that can affect your body weight. Certain medicines or medical conditions may affect your weight. Other factors include your:</p><ul><li>Genetic makeup</li><li>Eating habits</li><li>Sex</li><li>Race or ethnicity</li><li>Physical activity level</li></ul>How is <span class="qt0">obesity</span> diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have <span class="qt0">obesity</span>, your health care provider may:</p><ul><li>Ask about your health history, which may include reviewing your weight history, weight-loss efforts, and how physically active you are.</li><li>Do a physical exam, which may include checking your height, weight, and vital signs, as well as listening to your heart and lungs.</li><li>Order blood tests or other imaging tests, which may include checking any known health problems, as well as for other weight-related diseases and health conditions.</li><li>Calculate your BMI, to check your risk for certain diseases. The higher your BMI, the higher your risk. BMI does not distinguish between <span class="qt0">fat</span>, muscle, and bone mass. It may also overestimate body <span class="qt0">fat</span> in athletes or those with a muscular build, or underestimate body <span class="qt0">fat</span> in older persons, or others who have lost muscle.</li><li>Check your waist size, since a large waistline, with more body <span class="qt0">fat</span> around your abdomen (belly) rather than your hips, increases your risk for weight-related health problems.</li></ul>What health problems can <span class="qt0">obesity</span> cause?<p>Having a larger body size can make your heart work harder, put extra pressure on your joints, and may increase your risk for many health conditions, including:</p><ul><li>Type 2 diabetes.</li><li>Heart disease.</li><li>High blood pressure.</li><li>Stroke.</li><li>Metabolic syndrome.</li><li>Osteoarthritis.</li><li>Sleep apnea.</li><li>Pregnancy problems.</li><li>Fertility problems.</li><li>Some cancers.</li></ul><p>If you have <span class="qt0">obesity</span>, losing even 5 to 10% of your weight can delay or prevent some of these diseases. For example, that means losing 10 to 20 pounds if you weigh 200 pounds.</p>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0">obesity</span>?<p>Treatment plans for <span class="qt0">obesity</span> may depend on your overall weight, other health conditions, and your willingness to participate in a weight-loss plan. 

</p><p>Your provider can tell you what a healthy weight is for you, help you set goals, and give you tips on how to lose weight. They may refer you to other providers that specialize in nutrition or weight loss to help you make realistic goals and provide support. 

</p><p>Possible treatments may include:

</p><ul><li>Dietary changes and exercise goals to help you learn how to adopt healthy nutrition, exercise, and lifestyle changes to lose weight safely and keep it off long term.</li><li>Counseling or support groups can give you encouragement and help you understand what's behind weight changes.</li><li>Weight-loss medicines to treat <span class="qt0">obesity</span>.</li><li>Weight loss procedures or surgery if you have severe <span class="qt0">obesity</span> or serious <span class="qt0">obesity</span>-related health problems and have not been able to lose enough weight.</li></ul><p>A healthy lifestyle that includes healthy eating patterns and regular physical activity can help you lose weight and lower your chance of developing complications related to <span class="qt0">obesity</span>.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/obesityinchildren.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Obesity</span> in Children</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Childhood <span class="qt0">Obesity</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p><span class="qt0">Obesity</span> means having too much body <span class="qt0">fat</span>. It is different from being <span class="qt0">overweight</span>, which means weighing too much. Both terms mean that a person's weight is greater than what's considered healthy for his or her height.  Children grow at different rates, so it isn't always easy to know when a child has <span class="qt0">obesity or is overweight</span>. Ask your health care provider to check whether your child's weight and height are in a healthy range.</p><p>If a weight-loss program is necessary, involve the whole family in healthy habits so your child doesn't feel singled out.  Encourage healthy eating by:</p><ul><li>Serving more fruits and vegetables</li><li>Buying fewer soft drinks and high-<span class="qt0">fat</span>, high-calorie snack foods</li><li>Making sure your child eats breakfast every day</li><li>Eating fast food less often</li><li>Not using food as a reward</li></ul><p>Physical activity is also very important. Kids need about 60 minutes each day. It does not have to happen all at once. Several short periods of activity during the day are just as good.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/weightcontrol.html">
      <content name="title">Weight Control</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">BMI</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">Why is weight control important?<p>If you are struggling with your weight, you are not alone. In the United States, more than 70 percent of adults are <span class="qt0">overweight or have obesity</span>. Having this extra weight raises your risk for many health conditions, such as type 2 diabetes, heart disease, kidney disease, and certain cancers.</p><p>Reaching and staying at a healthy weight can be challenging. But having a healthy lifestyle, including healthy eating patterns and regular physical activity, can help you lose weight. It can also lower your chance of developing weight-related health conditions.</p>What factors affect weight and health?<p>You gain weight when you take in more calories (through food and drinks) than you use up from physical activity and daily living. But there are many different factors that can affect weight gain, such as:</p><ul><li>The world around you. Your home, community, and workplace all may affect how you make daily lifestyle choices. For example:
	<ul><li>It is often easier to find food and beverages high in calories, sugar, and <span class="qt0">fat</span>. For instance, vending machines, cafeterias, and special events may not offer healthy, lower calorie options.</li><li>Less healthy foods may be cheaper than healthier foods.</li><li>Many people are getting less physical activity because they are spending more time using smartphones and other devices.</li></ul>
</li><li>Families. <span class="qt0">Overweight and obesity</span> tend to run in families. This suggests that genes may play a role in weight gain. Families may also share eating and lifestyle habits. For example, some families may often have foods and drinks that are high in calories, sugar, and <span class="qt0">fat</span>. And some families may tend to be less active and spend more time doing things like sitting and watching TV or using computers.</li><li>Not enough sleep. People who don't get enough sleep may eat more calories and snack more.</li><li>Emotions. Some people eat when they feel bored, sad, or stressed, even if they are not hungry.</li><li>Medicines and health conditions. Taking certain medicines, such as steroids and certain antidepressants, can lead to weight gain. Some chronic health problems can also cause you to gain weight. A few examples are Cushing syndrome and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).</li></ul>How can I get to and stay at a healthy weight?<p>Getting to and staying at a healthy weight involves finding a balance of food and activity. To lose weight, you need to take in fewer calories than you use up. Some ways to do this are:</p><ul><li>Eating more nutrient-rich foods, such as foods with lots of vitamins, minerals, and fiber.</li><li>Eating and drinking less of the foods and beverages that have lots of calories, salt, sugar, and <span class="qt0">fat</span>.</li><li>Limiting alcohol.</li><li>Finding healthier ways to cook, such as using healthier oils to cook with and baking or grilling instead of frying foods.</li><li>Getting more physical activity. The general recommendation is for adults to get 150 minutes of physical activity each week. This time can be broken down into short bursts of activity throughout your day. Types of physical activity include: 
	<ul><li>Aerobic activity, which is also called cardio. It uses your large muscle groups (chest, legs, and back) to speed up your heart rate and breathing.</li><li>Muscle-strengthening activity, which is also called strength training. It works your muscles by making you push or pull against something.</li></ul>
</li></ul><p>You may decide to do these lifestyle changes on your own, or you may decide to try a weight-loss diet or program. Before you start, it's important to check with your health care provider first. Your provider can tell you what a healthy weight is for you, help you set goals, and give you tips on how to lose weight.</p>What are weight management medicines?<p>If making lifestyle changes or doing a weight-loss program are not enough to help you lose weight, your provider may prescribe medicines. These medicines are meant to help people who have weight-related health conditions and should be used along with healthy eating and physical activity. The prescription medicines to treat <span class="qt0">overweight and obesity</span> work in different ways. Some may help you feel less hungry or full sooner. Others may make it harder for your body to absorb <span class="qt0">fat</span> from the foods you eat.</p><p>Another treatment is weight loss surgery. Your provider may recommend the surgery if you have severe <span class="qt0">obesity</span> or serious <span class="qt0">obesity</span>-related health problems and you have not been able to lose enough weight.</p>How can I maintain my weight loss?<p>Maintaining weight loss can be challenging, and it's normal to slip back into old habits sometimes. The key is to keep a healthy balance of food and activity that works for you. Checking your weight regularly can help you notice small changes early and stay on track. And if you have a setback, don't be discouraged, simply refocus on your healthy habits and keep going.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/diabetes.html">
      <content name="title">Diabetes</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Diabetes Mellitus</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Sugar Diabetes</content>
      <content name="altTitle">DM</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is diabetes?<p>Diabetes, also known as diabetes mellitus, is a disease in which your blood glucose, or blood sugar, levels are too high. Glucose is your body's main source of energy. Your body can make glucose, but it also comes from the food you eat. Insulin is a hormone made by your pancreas. Insulin helps move glucose from your bloodstream into your cells, where it can be used for energy.</p><p>If you have diabetes, your body can't make insulin, can't use insulin as well as it should, or both. Too much glucose stays in your blood and doesn't reach your cells. This can cause glucose levels to get too high. Over time, high blood glucose levels can lead to serious health conditions. But you can take steps to manage your diabetes and try to prevent these health problems.</p>What are the types of diabetes?<p>There are different types of diabetes:</p><ul><li>Type 1 diabetes. If you have type 1 diabetes, your body makes little or no insulin. It happens when your immune system attacks and destroys the cells that produce insulin. </li><li>Type 2 diabetes. This is the most common form of diabetes. If you have type 2 diabetes, your body may still be able to make insulin, but your cells don't respond well to insulin. They can't easily take up enough glucose from your blood.</li><li>Gestational diabetes. This is a form of diabetes that develops during pregnancy. It happens when your body can't make the extra insulin it needs during pregnancy.</li></ul>What causes diabetes?<p>The different types of diabetes have different causes:</p><ul><li>Researchers think type 1 diabetes is caused by genes and factors in the environment that might trigger the disease.</li><li>Type 2 diabetes is caused by several factors, including lifestyle factors and genes. The lifestyle factors include not being physically active and being <span class="qt0">overweight</span> or having <span class="qt0">obesity</span>.</li><li>Researchers think gestational diabetes is caused by the hormonal changes of pregnancy along with genetic and lifestyle factors.</li></ul>Who is more likely to develop diabetes?<p>The different types of diabetes have different risk factors:</p><ul><li>You can develop type 1 diabetes at any age, but it most often starts in childhood. Having a parent or sibling with type 1 diabetes may increase your chance of developing it.</li><li>You are at higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes if you:</li><ul><li>Are <span class="qt0">overweight or have obesity</span>.</li><li>Are over age 35. Children, teenagers, and younger adults can get diabetes, but it is more common in middle-aged and older adults.</li><li>Have a family history of diabetes.</li><li>Have prediabetes. This means that your blood glucose is higher than normal, but it's not high enough to be called diabetes.</li><li>Had gestational diabetes.</li><li>Have given birth to a baby weighing 9 pounds or more.</li><li>Are African American, American Indian, Asian American, Hispanic/Latino, or Pacific Islander.</li><li>Are not physically active.</li><li>Have certain other health conditions, such as high blood pressure or polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).</li></ul><li>You are at higher risk of developing gestational diabetes if you:</li><ul><li>Are <span class="qt0">overweight or have obesity</span>.</li><li>Have a family history of diabetes.</li><li>Had gestational diabetes in a previous pregnancy.</li><li>Have given birth to a baby weighing 9 pounds or more.</li><li>Have polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).</li><li>Are African American, Hispanic/Latino, American Indian, Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian, or Pacific Islander.</li></ul></ul>What are the symptoms of diabetes?<p>The symptoms of diabetes may include:</p><ul><li>Feeling very thirsty</li><li>Feeling very hungry</li><li>Urinating (peeing) more often, including at night</li><li>Fatigue</li><li>Blurry vision</li><li>Numbness or tingling in the feet or hands</li><li>Sores that do not heal</li><li>Losing weight without trying</li></ul><p>But it's important to know that your symptoms may vary, depending on which type you have:</p><ul><li>The symptoms of type 1 diabetes usually come on quickly and can be severe.</li><li>With type 2 diabetes, the symptoms often develop slowly, over several years. The symptoms can be so mild that you might not even notice them.</li><li>Gestational diabetes often has no symptoms. If you do have symptoms, they may be mild. If you are pregnant, you will usually be screened for this condition between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy. </li></ul>How is diabetes diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have diabetes, your health care provider will use one or more glucose blood tests. There are several types, including the A1C test.</p>What are the treatments for diabetes?<p>Treatment for diabetes involves managing your blood glucose levels:</p><ul><li>If you have type 1 diabetes, you will need to take daily doses of insulin, either by injection or through a special pump. Some people also need to take another type of diabetes medicine that works with insulin.</li><li>If you have type 2 diabetes, you may be able to manage or even reverse it by making lifestyle changes. These include eating a healthy diet, staying at healthy weight, and getting regular physical activity. Some people also need to take diabetes medicines to manage their diabetes.</li><li>If you have gestational diabetes, you may be able to lower your glucose levels by eating a healthy diet and getting regular exercise. But be sure to talk to your provider about your treatment options. Gestational diabetes usually goes away after you give birth. But you will have a higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes later.</li></ul><p>Checking your blood glucose levels is also an important part of managing your diabetes. Ask your provider about the best way to check your blood glucose level and how often you should check it.</p>Can diabetes be prevented?<p>Type 1 diabetes can't be prevented.</p><p>You may be able to delay or prevent type 2 diabetes through the same lifestyle changes that are used to manage diabetes (eating a healthy diet, staying at a healthy weight, and getting regular physical activity). These lifestyle changes may also help prevent gestational diabetes.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>
